question.text: India deposited its instrument of ratification of the Multilateral Instrument (MLI) with OECD on 25 June 2019 (in force from 1 October 2019). From a Cat II AIF manager's perspective advising non-resident LPs, what is the MOST important substantive change the MLI brings to India's treaty network?

answer.text: Automatic withdrawal of all treaty benefits for non-residents
A new TDS rate of 20% on every outbound payment
Mandatory 5% India-resident investor participation limit in every AIF
Introduction of the Principal Purpose Test (PPT) / LOB-type tests to deny treaty benefits where obtaining benefit is one of the principal purposes of an arrangement (BEPS Action 6)

explanation.text: **The Logic:** The MLI implements BEPS Action 6 (Prevention of Treaty Abuse). Its centrepiece is the Principal Purpose Test (PPT) — treaty benefits are denied if it is reasonable to conclude that obtaining the benefit was one of the principal purposes of the arrangement, unless granting the benefit is in accordance with the object and purpose of the treaty. Many treaties also include LOB (Limitation of Benefits). India signed on 7 June 2017 with 66 others; India's positions are now notified under Section 90(1) of the ITA. **The Trap:** Option A — the MLI does NOT cancel treaties wholesale. Option B — invents a TDS rate. Option C — confuses MLI with Section 9A conditions. **Cross-Exam Context:** XV and XIX-A touch on BEPS at concept level; XIX-C requires the manager to run PPT analysis when structuring feeder funds. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Document a 'commercial substance' file for every NR LP claiming treaty benefit: board minutes, physical presence, employee count, economic rationale. In a PPT challenge, documentation from CONTEMPORANEOUSLY produced evidence is the difference between keeping the treaty benefit and losing it.
